voyage.title: Bartolomeu Dias Rounds the Cape (1487-1488)
voyage.ships: two caravels and a storeship, the first ever sent south with supplies
voyage.sponsor: sailing from Lisbon for King John II of Portugal
voyage.summary: The voyage that proved the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean were one sea. South past the last padrao of Cao, then a fortnight blown out of sight of land by a southerly gale — and when Dias turned east he found no coast, because he had passed the continent's end without seeing it. He came back north to a coastline running east, followed it as far as the Great Fish River, and was made to turn home by a crew who had had enough. He named the headland the Cape of Storms; the king renamed it the Cape of Good Hope.
voyage.what_was_lost: Everything Dias wrote. The Casa da India held the logs, the charts and the sailing directions of the Portuguese discoveries, and the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 destroyed the archive along with a third of the city. No journal of this voyage survives, no chart drawn on it, and no word from any of the men aboard. What we have is Joao de Barros, writing his Decadas da Asia around 1552 from papers that burned two centuries later — so even the chronicle cannot now be checked against what it read. The dates below are his, the landfalls are his, and where he was vague this atlas is vague too.

waypoints.event: Two caravels and a storeship leave the Tagus. The storeship is the innovation: no Portuguese expedition had been provisioned to go this far.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: Joao de Barros, Decadas da Asia (c. 1552), as reconstructed by modern scholarship

waypoints.event: The Portuguese fort on the Gold Coast, the last certain landfall before the unknown coast.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: Joao de Barros, Decadas da Asia (c. 1552), as reconstructed by modern scholarship

waypoints.event: Diogo Cao's furthest padrao, and the end of the known world. Everything south of here is new.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: Joao de Barros, Decadas da Asia (c. 1552), as reconstructed by modern scholarship

waypoints.event: A padrao raised. The storeship is left here with nine men; when Dias returns, three are alive.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: Joao de Barros, Decadas da Asia (c. 1552), as reconstructed by modern scholarship

waypoints.place_modern: open ocean, south-west of the Cape
waypoints.date_note: about thirteen days, January 1488; position unknown
waypoints.event: A southerly gale takes them out of sight of land for a fortnight. This is the stage nobody can place: the position here is an inference from how long they ran and how fast, and it is drawn as one.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: Joao de Barros, Decadas da Asia (c. 1552), as reconstructed by modern scholarship

waypoints.event: Turning east they find no coast, so they turn north — and strike land running east, not south. They have passed the end of Africa without seeing it.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: Joao de Barros, Decadas da Asia (c. 1552), as reconstructed by modern scholarship

waypoints.event: A padrao raised on an island in the bay. The coast keeps running east: the way to India is open.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: Joao de Barros, Decadas da Asia (c. 1552), as reconstructed by modern scholarship

waypoints.event: The crew refuse to go further. Dias turns back here, within reach of the thing he had come to prove and unable to prove it.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: Joao de Barros, Decadas da Asia (c. 1552), as reconstructed by modern scholarship

waypoints.place_modern: Cape of Good Hope, South Africa
waypoints.event: Only on the way home does he see the headland he had passed in the storm. He calls it the Cape of Storms; the king, hearing what it means, renames it the Cape of Good Hope.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: Joao de Barros, Decadas da Asia (c. 1552), as reconstructed by modern scholarship

waypoints.event: Home. Ten years later Vasco da Gama sails the road Dias opened, and Dias goes with him as far as the Cape Verde islands before turning back.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: Joao de Barros, Decadas da Asia (c. 1552), as reconstructed by modern scholarship
